channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of June 10-16, 1985 — Summer Games II and Winter Games headline the post-CES games slate
item.description: Epyx adds a second summer contest and a winter programme as Lucasfilm adventures line up behind the sports crowd. The home computer is heading back to the stadium. Reporting from the Chicago Summer Consumer Electronics Show, Popular Computing Weekly’s June 13–19 edition puts Epyx’s Summer Games II and Winter Games at the front of a busy games slate. The show took place June 2–5; the news reaching readers this week is a preview of the months ahead. Also this week: Amiga preview raises the stakes against Atari and Macintosh · Amstrad aims its 128K CPC at the American home · Poet Robert Pinsky takes the text adventure into the electronic novel.

item.title: Week of June 3-9, 1985 — Nintendo brings a robot to its new Entertainment System
item.description: At Summer CES, Nintendo recasts its American proposal as an entertainment system, not a home-computer kit. CHICAGO — Nintendo is giving its proposed American video-game system a new calling card: a robot. At the June Summer Consumer Electronics Show, the company is presenting the Nintendo Entertainment System with a Robotic Operating Buddy, a conspicuous bid to win attention on a retail floor still wary of video games. Also this week: Atari packs an encyclopedia onto an optical disc · ST and Commodore 128 approach stores, but delivery promises still matter · A poet takes on the text-adventure establishment.

item.title: Week of May 27-June 2, 1985 — Apple merges divisions; Jobs loses Macintosh command
item.description: May 31 realignment centralizes operations under Sculley; co-founder remains chairman. Apple has stripped Steve Jobs of operational command of its Macintosh division in a major realignment announced Friday, May 31. The Macintosh and Apple II divisions are being merged, while marketing and manufacturing are centralized to remove overlapping functions. John Sculley remains president and chief executive officer. Also this week: Championship Lode Runner challenges the veterans · GEM brings the graphical desktop to IBM and Atari · MacVision turns video into Macintosh pictures.

item.title: Week of May 20-26, 1985 — Fifty punishing rooms put Lode Runner veterans to the test
item.description: Brøderbund’s advanced sequel trades the construction kit for fifty hard-won puzzles. Brøderbund has a demanding assignment for players who have exhausted Lode Runner: fifty more rooms, built to punish complacency. Championship Lode Runner is the subject of Michael B. Williams’s review in the May issue of COMPUTE!, and its audience is the veteran rather than the newcomer. The original game’s 150 screens form the apprenticeship; this collection is the examination. Also this week: GEM promises a graphical bridge between IBM PCs and Atari · MacVision turns videotape and camera pictures into Macintosh illustrations · Synapse sells adventures as electronic novels.

item.title: Week of May 13-19, 1985 — Mastertronic pitches Commodore games at $9.99
item.description: A $9.99 price tag brings a fresh budget pitch to the Commodore 64 shelf. Mastertronic is making price the attraction on the Commodore 64 games rack. The May issue of COMPUTE! reports games at $9.99 apiece, a modest entry ticket for owners looking beyond the familiar full-price boxes. This is the month’s product-news coverage, not a claim that the games all arrived during this particular week. Also this week: Atari rejoins Summer CES; ST clears FCC hurdle · GEM brings the desktop metaphor to PCs and Atari · Star offers near-letter-quality printing from $299.

item.title: Week of May 6-12, 1985 — Championship Lode Runner turns veterans into certified champions
item.description: Brøderbund’s fifty-screen challenge gives veteran runners a certificate to chase. Championship Lode Runner asks a pointed question of anyone who has mastered the original: can you survive fifty screens built for experts? Brøderbund’s sequel, reviewed in the May COMPUTE!, trades the original’s 150 screens for a smaller, deliberately demanding collection. This is a test of seasoned runners, not a gentle first lesson in collecting gold and evading guards. Also this week: Atari’s attack: 520ST reaches the hands-on test bench · Sidekick puts the desk inside the PC — at two prices · MacVision imports the video world into Macintosh documents.

item.title: Week of April 29-May 5, 1985 — Build a robot, solve an adventure: programming becomes play
item.description: Robot Odyssey I and Chipwits make circuits and visual instructions the machinery of adventure. Adventure games are putting a new question to the home computer: can the player build the intelligence that wins the game? In the April–May Computer Gaming World, Gregg Williams compares Robot Odyssey I and Chipwits, two simulations that make programming itself the entertainment. These are current review selections, not announcements of releases during this week. Also this week: AT competition widens: three rivals promise more choice · Buyers and vendors still divided over software protection · Share a screen over the telephone.

item.title: Week of April 22-28, 1985 — Gribbly’s Day Out brings airborne rescue to the Commodore screen
item.description: Hewson’s unusual rescue game earns a lively reception in this week’s home-computer press. A rescue mission takes a strange and expressive turn on the Commodore screen. Gribbly’s Day Out, from Hewson, sends its hero after young gribblets, mixing movement on land with Psi-powered flight. The review in this week’s Home Computing Weekly treats the result as an inventive departure from routine arcade action. Also this week: Amstrad puts disc storage at the center of its new home micro · Chuckie Egg packaging turns to holograms against copying · Atari’s announced ST machines promise a graphical desktop at home-computer prices.

item.title: Week of April 15-21, 1985 — Fifty Mission Crush puts the B-17 campaign on home computers
item.description: SSI trades arcade spectacle for the fortunes of a bomber crew in April’s simulation review. A home-computer flight need not be a test of reflexes. Strategic Simulations’ Fifty Mission Crush makes the player responsible for an Eighth Air Force B-17 and the men aboard it. James V. Trunzo’s April COMPUTE! review finds its pull in a campaign of decisions and consequences rather than lavish graphics. Also this week: Commons passes software-copyright bill at third reading · Atari promises a mouse-and-window computer for $599 · Commodore 128 promises three ways to preserve a software library.

item.title: Week of April 8-14, 1985 — Fifty missions, one crew: the bomber game that makes survival count
item.description: SSI turns the B-17 campaign into a test of preparation, persistence and crew survival. Britain is the starting point, but keeping a B-17 and its crew alive is the real destination. Strategic Simulations’ Fifty Mission Crush puts the player in command of an Eighth Air Force bomber for a campaign of fifty missions over Germany, France and the Netherlands. James V. Trunzo’s April COMPUTE! review finds its appeal in sustained command rather than a quick burst of arcade action. Also this week: Atari and Commodore promise a bargain-computer generation · Home-computer optimism meets the PCjr reckoning · Pooh opens the adventure door without a parser battle.

item.title: Week of April 1-7, 1985 — Atari’s ST gathers support as the 16-bit challenge approaches
item.description: April 6 cover coverage puts GEM and the new Atari machines in the spotlight; availability remains a forecast. Atari’s new 16-bit computers are gathering an audience before they reach ordinary desks. Personal Computer News makes the machines its April 6 cover story, pointing to GEM and growing support for the platform. It is a week of anticipation, not a verified retail launch. Also this week: Commodore 128 promises three computing worlds without abandoning the 64 · Disney and Sierra make adventure gaming accessible to younger players · A B-17 campaign in fifteen-minute installments · SpeedScript 3.0 brings a machine-language word processor to expanded VIC-20s.

item.title: Week of March 25-31, 1985 — Solo Flight puts a mail route inside a home-computer cockpit
item.description: Best sourced gaming feature; a March review, not a newly verified release. A mail route gives the home pilot a reason to take off. MicroProse’s Solo Flight, reviewed in this month’s COMPUTE!, puts navigation, weather and delivery decisions inside a light-airplane simulation. Sid Meier’s program is listed for the Commodore 64 and Atari computers with at least 48K, a disk drive and joystick, at a publisher price of $34.95. Also this week: After IBM’s PCjr retreat, home-computer owners weigh compatibility and support · A $12.95 disk challenges the commercial word processor · Jazz misses its late-March date as Macintosh waits for office software.

item.title: Week of March 18-24, 1985 — IBM pulls the plug on PCjr production
item.description: March 19 announcement ends a bid for the mass-market home computer. IBM announced March 19 that production of its PCjr home computer would end in April. UPI’s Boca Raton dispatch attributes the decision to slack sales, bringing a sharp change of course for the company’s consumer-computer effort. Also this week: Solo Flight puts the mail run in the pilot’s hands · A six-kilobyte word processor arrives in the magazine · The Print Shop makes the home printer earn its keep · One screen for the computer and the evening television.

item.title: Week of March 11-17, 1985 — Symbolics registers the first .com address
item.description: The Lisp-workstation maker enters the domain register on March 15. Massachusetts workstation maker Symbolics registered symbolics.com on March 15, establishing the first registration under the .com domain. It is a small administrative entry in computer networking, rather than the opening of a new public information service. Also this week: Solo Flight makes the home computer a mail pilot’s cockpit · ConnNet opens Connecticut dial-up route to information services · SpeedScript 3.0 puts a substantial word processor in a magazine · Color printing moves below $300.

item.title: Week of March 4-10, 1985 — SSI sends strategy gamers into space and World War II
item.description: SSI puts diplomacy, conquest and battlefield command on the home computer. Strategy players have two very different maps to unfold. March COMPUTE! reports that Strategic Simulations has introduced Imperium Galactum and Field of Fire, pairing a contest for interstellar power with command of an infantry company in World War II. Each carries a suggested retail price of $39.95. Also this week: SpeedScript 3.0 brings a 6K word processor to magazine readers · Color printing breaks below $300 · 2400-bps modems promise speed, but supply and service costs loom.

item.title: Week of February 25-March 3, 1985 — Inside King’s Quest: $700,000 buys a new kind of adventure
item.description: February reporting opens the workshop behind Sierra’s ambitious adventure. A kingdom of 80 scenes comes at a very real price. Donald B. Trivette’s February COMPUTE! account puts the cost of Sierra’s King’s Quest above $700,000, with Roberta Williams and six programmers and artists working for 18 months. IBM supplied a prototype PCjr and asked for a game that could show its color graphics before the machine was announced. Also this week: Rent a PC for a month—but whose software license goes with it? · Michael Crichton takes storytelling from the cinema to Amazon · PC-Write asks users to share the software—and pays registered referrers · Online rivals bring games and conversation below three dollars an hour.

item.title: Week of February 18-24, 1985 — Inside King's Quest: the $700,000 adventure behind the PCjr's animated kingdom
item.description: February reporting opens the workshop behind Sierra’s ambitious adventure. A kingdom of 80 scenes comes at a very real price. Donald B. Trivette’s February COMPUTE! account puts the cost of Sierra’s King’s Quest above $700,000, with Roberta Williams and six programmers and artists working for 18 months. IBM supplied a prototype PCjr and asked for a game that could show its color graphics before the machine was announced. Also this week: Michael Crichton takes storytelling from the cinema to Amazon · PC-EYE brings video capture and pixel retouching to the IBM PC · PC-Write asks users to share the software—and pays registered referrers.

item.title: Week of February 11-17, 1985 — Michael Crichton trades the movie screen for the adventure game
item.description: In a February interview, the author behind Amazon explains why story should guide the player. Michael Crichton wants the computer adventure to tell a story, not merely conceal a solution. Interviewed by Betsy Staples in February’s Creative Computing, the novelist and filmmaker describes Amazon, his Trillium Software adventure made with programmer Stephen Warady, as a sequence of dramatic episodes. Also this week: A $239 color printer meets the real-paper test · The Commodore 64 becomes a music room for non-musicians · IBM announces its 3090 mainframe family.

item.title: Week of February 4-10, 1985 — Michael Crichton wants adventure games to make sense
item.description: February’s COMPUTE! finds the novelist building adventures around believable solutions, not magic words. Michael Crichton has a complaint familiar to anyone stranded at an adventure-game prompt: a sensible solution ought not to fail merely because the player has guessed the wrong words. In February’s COMPUTE!, the novelist discusses Amazon and argues for puzzles that answer to the logic of the situation rather than an arbitrary phrase. Also this week: Wozniak leaves daily Apple duties for a living-room video venture · Online games and conversation challenge the established services · PC-Write turns copying into a sales channel.

item.title: Week of January 28-February 3, 1985 — Commodore earnings plunge 94%; home-computer boom faces its reckoning
item.description: Quarterly profit shrinks to $3.2 million as the industry searches for its next reason to buy. Commodore’s latest figures have put a hard number on the cooling home-computer boom. Paul Richter reports in the February 1 Los Angeles Times that quarterly profit fell 94 percent to $3.2 million. Sales for the quarter ended December 31 declined 21 percent from a year earlier, to $338.7 million. Also this week: TurboTape promises disk-like loading from ordinary Commodore cassettes · The C64 becomes a six-track music studio · JTERM’s new version brings 1200-bps access to Atari bulletin-board callers.
